beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: [Schedule your personal agent](exercises/personal-agent-homework.md) to read your challenge memory for a week.

beats.trigger: **Evaluate** when splitting pays off and when one agent wins

beats.trigger: Three agents search Confluence, OneDrive and practitioner articles, and three more decide what it means.
beats.got: Six agents on my own company's documents. I'd want to know first whether IT has approved that.

beats.trigger: The agent writes the message first and sends only after approval.
beats.got: The risk is named up front and a human approves before anything leaves. That is a control I can accept.

beats.trigger: Push back when the first answer restates the problem.
beats.got: I get an agent to name the one thing blocking my problem. Maybe useful, but I can't tell what it saves.

beats.trigger: Skip any retriever you can't run today.

beats.trigger: **Close. Does this feel right?**

beats.trigger: When do you split, and how?
beats.got: A question I can follow. It sounds like a make-or-buy decision.

beats.trigger: A hundred tiny agents cost more to coordinate than they save.
beats.got: There is a cost curve, but it comes with no figures.

beats.trigger: Splitting adds coordination cost: handoffs, mis-framing, prompts to tune per agent, a synthesis step that can mislead.
beats.got: The training names the downside before I had to ask. Default to one agent. It's the first honest thing today.

beats.trigger: A legal-policy agent shouldn't have customer-data access.
beats.got: There are three tests for splitting. Access is the one that matters to me, because it is a control question.

beats.trigger: Split for a reason, not because "three is more thorough".
beats.got: More agents are not more rigour. That's the answer to a vendor pitch.

beats.trigger: The synthesizer then commits to one diagnosis and drops what does not serve it.
beats.got: Without a framework the output is a blend. With one it picks. I can't tell yet whether it picks correctly.

beats.trigger: Could one prompt produce the same quality of output? If yes, write that one prompt.
beats.got: A test I can apply to any proposal where someone wants to spend more. One question: could one prompt do it?

beats.trigger: **Helper agents in one session (the Phase 2 move).**
beats.got: There are two ways to build it. That's an IT matter for me. No cost difference is given.

beats.trigger: One agent can call another for a different stance, source zone, or working style.

beats.trigger: A retriever finds two numbers and the curator keeps one.

beats.trigger: If one well-prompted agent does the job, write that prompt.

beats.trigger: Agents get stuck: wrong source, three views averaged into mush, the wrong file written, confident right before a failed handoff.

beats.trigger: move the risky step from "do" to "propose."

beats.trigger: Agents add non-deterministic behaviour, prompt injection (direct, or inside retrieved text) and emergent capability you can only bound.
beats.got: Risk is named and it sits on top of normal security. This is what I'd bring to IT.

beats.trigger: An agent that works across connected systems has access to those systems.

beats.trigger: add an agent for a critical dependency, or a plan visualisation.

take_homes: Default to one agent. Split only for different access, dialect or stance, and ask whether one prompt could do the same job.
Handoffs between agents are where figures get lost or dropped, and nothing in this module checks that the final briefing is true.
Before any agent gets finance data, ask what is the worst it could do with that access.

monday.move: Ask my controller to try the month-end variance commentary with one agent, proposing only and not posting anywhere.
monday.when: after IT has approved the tool for finance data, not before
monday.stop_condition: If the commentary contains a figure that doesn't match the ledger, or if I can't see where each number came from, I stop.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data.

misconception.why: All day nothing said what a deployment costs per month or what the organisation has to build to run it. The module spoke of workflows and files, but the tool still looks like a licence I buy. The honesty about coordination cost and unchecked output made me trust the trainer a bit more, but it didn't change that view.

one_line: Honest about when not to use it, and the 'start with don't' rule is worth having. But there was no cost figure and no way to check the answer, and a CFO leaves with nothing to defend to the board.
